Outcome_variable.evidence_source: [/page/8/Text/8] Because life satisfaction, psychological well-being, and neuroticism were correlated in the FLSA data set, it is possible that the apparent interaction between neuroticism and yearly life-satisfaction variation was caused by a quadratic relationship between life satisfaction and psychological well-being. [/page/9/Text/6] In the second set of supplemental analyses, psychological well-being was transformed to correct for skew and heteroscedasticity. I attempted several linear and spline transformations following the work of Snijders and Bosker (2012) and found that the best solution—that is, the solution for which residuals in the unconditional model were most homoscedastic—was a linear cube transformation. This analysis repeated the main model sequence (Models 1–5) with psychological well-being3 as the outcome variable

ethnicity.evidence_source: [/page/8/Text/10] Similarly, African American participants reported higher psychological well-being than White participants (b = 0.229, SE = 0.056, p < .001) and may have reported a weaker within-person correlation between yearly variation in life satisfaction and yearly psychological wellbeing (Race × Life Satisfaction interaction; b = −0.054, SE = 0.029, p = .06).

lag.evidence_source: [/page/8/Text/6] The first set of analyses added variables to Model 5 to account for quadratic life-satisfaction effects, time, demographics, and other personality traits. The key questions in these models were (a) whether the additional variables had unique effects of their own and (b) whether the additional variables accounted for the interaction between neuroticism and yearly variation in life satisfaction. [/page/8/Text/9] Time. The full expanded model indicated a small main effect for years in study (b = 0.008, SE = 0.003, p = .011).
